rv.q: And while I entered the theater a skeptic, in fact the production, directed by the busy Jamie Lloyd, is not a gimmicky fiasco but a visually striking and unusually tender staging of the celebrated “tragicomedy,” which dramatizes the echoing loneliness of human experience.
It’s their Godot, and damned if it doesn’t work.
Gilmour’s set—simultaneously a gesture to Fascist architecture, a conduit to nowhere, and a scatological joke—shores up the production in several ways.

Frankly, it’s hard to believe anyone in the theater will crave another half hour beyond the available two and I doubt this revival will loom large in anyone’s long-term memory, notwithstanding the plethora of interesting takes.
They don’t need a production to confine them further.
This lower temperature approach too often misses the work's humor, horror and emotional resonance.
But New Yorkers who have seen more seasoned stage actors in the roles in more penetrating productions
Neither especially funny, emotional or thought-provoking, it’s caught in a sort of aesthetically pleasing but hollow limbo.

But though Thornton turns Lucky’s famously impermeable monologue – an erudite-seeming rambling on the command to “think!” – into a spellbinding swirl, there’s a ghoulish, overdone quality to their intrusions that tip the show into uncomfortable sensory overwhelm.

The pleasant prospect of seeing Reeves and Winter together makes this production to some extent critic-proof—and anyhow, this is a play in which “Crritic!” is the worst insult that Estragon can think up.
This particularly meandering and stiff “Godot” is hardly an excellent adventure.
For the most part here, he doesn't seem to have anything to say. That's disappointing on its own.
Their relationship is built to last, even in a Buñuelian hellscape that will, we know, keep going and going.
Back in New York with a starry cast, Waiting for Godot makes you think about meaning in an indifferent world, and that’s a timely takeaway.
Transfixing performances from Winter and Reeves that help you look past the production's shortcomings.
Their endless adventure in Beckett's wasteland is a strange, curious, and surprisingly affecting experiment.

If there’s a deeper meaning bleeding out from Lloyd’s revival, perhaps it’s this production’s exploration of how desperately we try to grapple with the passing of time, toiling to turn each ephemeral moment into a scene worth playing.

Lloyd's Godot makes plenty of fascinating choices, some more effective than others. The characters often stare back at the audience; the tree is nowhere to be seen; the props are pantomimed; and there is a throwaway reference to Bill & Ted, equally likely to elicit chuckles as it is to yank you from the play's subject matter back into a world wh...
Neither one of them is reinventing the wheel, and neither is Lloyd.

Reeves and Winter make you feel it when the men embrace—as if one is holding on to the life raft embodied by the other—and when they quietly care for each other, strange day after strange day. If this is stunt casting, then it is stunt casting with a sweetened depth.
It is not a performance, and Reeves very studied and mannered delivery of his lines is enough to ban the word “staccato” from Webster’s.
But I would have rather spent a longer time with a Godot helmed by a director more concerned about what he wanted to say than how differently he could say it.
But they don’t come close to truly conveying the characters’ existential despair, nor their vaudevillian-style clowning.

Despite the shortcomings of the leads’ muted performances and some questionable directorial choices, this Godot does have a comic energy and conveys a hint of Beckett’s bleak vision of humanity’s eternal quandary in seeking meaning where none seems to exist.
But director Jamie Lloyd could have done a lot worse than recapture the humor of those goofy characters Bill and Ted in more than just that one moment.
Let it be known: I recoiled more times during “A Big Bold Beautiful Journey” than at “House of 1000. Corpses.”
Here, the pair’s well-meaning performances, combined with Beckett’s ultra-dense text, end up being far more successful at periodically boring us than delighting us.
Tedious for them, and sometimes for us.
“Waiting for Godot” was subpar, forgettable, and dull.

cn.t: Critics find this Reeves-Winter reunion a visually striking but uneven "Godot" that capitalizes on Bill & Ted nostalgia with mixed results. Lloyd's stylish direction divides opinion, though the duo's chemistry earns praise.

sg.ra: SeatPlan, TickPick and Headout all converge: center rows D-K sit at a perfect distance to take in the whole stage without craning. Row A is called out as too close for comfortable viewing. Dress Circle overhangs at Orchestra row L and the Mezz overhang only becomes obvious at row R without significantly cutting the stage, so the middle band is protected. 2017 ATG restoration upgraded legroom throughout.

SeatPlan flags Dress Circle A-B center as offering unobstructed sightlines and the 'front few rows of the Center Dress Circle' as premium; rows D-F center are repeatedly called out as great-value seats with full sweep of the stage. The 258-seat section has a good rake and generous legroom. Balcony overhang only becomes obvious at row J and doesn't cut into the stage, so every row is usable.

SeatPlan describes Balcony rows A-B center as hanging close enough for detailed views and reports sightlines 'better than average' for a third level. Rear rows G-H are the cheapest in the house. Rake is very good, but legroom is tighter than the rest of the theater and the top of the stage may be cut by the balcony's angle. AVFMS user at G110 noted that some in-audience action isn't visible from rear balcony.

vr.q: I liked the production but I feel lukewarm about the play... while I don't think this production could sell me on the play as a whole, I still think it was solid.
If you love this play or have never seen this play, I wouldn't recommend this production of it for you.
